venue_now: ACL 2025 (Long Papers), pp. 16593-16615, per notes/cited_set_resolution.md; the text is arXiv v2 (26 May 2025, p. 1) and has no venue header
what_it_is: PhysReason is a 1,200-problem physics benchmark. A quarter of the problems are knowledge-based; the rest are reasoning problems split evenly into easy, medium and hard. They come from college entrance exams, practice tests and international physics olympiads, filtered to exclude any whose solution a five-minute Google search finds (pp. 1, 3). Every problem has an annotated step-by-step solution that gives, for each step, the theorem used, the target quantity, the formula and the value. Solutions average 8.1 steps (15.6 for hard problems), and 81% of problems include diagrams (pp. 1-4). Its Physics Solution Auto-Scoring framework scores answers (PSAS-A) and steps (PSAS-S). For each annotated step, an LLM extracts the model's corresponding work and scores formula and value at half weight each; it also locates the first error step and classifies it into one of seven error types (pp. 4-5). On 1,000 manually annotated model solutions, PSAS with DeepSeek-V3 matches the annotation on 99.35% of answer judgements and 98.04% of first-error-step locations, against 33-38% for direct LLM evaluation (Table 2, p. 6). All 15 evaluated models score below 60% at answer level, falling from 75.11% on knowledge problems to 31.95% on hard ones (p. 1).
domain: physics (classical, quantum and fluid mechanics, thermodynamics, electromagnetics, optics, relativity) at college-entrance-exam and olympiad level; multimodal (81% of problems have diagrams)
size: 1,200 problems (300 knowledge, 300 each easy, medium and hard) covering 147 theorems, plus a 200-problem PhysReason-mini; 15 models (7 non-O-like, 8 O-like) (pp. 1-3, 6)
source_of_items: exams and competitions: public problems from Chinese, Indian and Russian college entrance exams and their practice tests, and from IPhO, APhO, EPhO and others, drawn from 1,254 PDFs holding over 20,000 problems. Parsed with MinerU and deduplicated; translations checked by engineering PhD candidates (p. 3)
has_gold_traces: yes: each annotation includes a step-by-step Solution and a Step Analysis giving the theorem, target, formula and value of every step (Figure 1, p. 2; section 3.2, p. 3; App. B.2, pp. 14-15); PSAS-S scores model steps against them (p. 5)
evaluation: LLM judge at two levels. PSAS-A (answer level): an LLM extracts each sub-question's answer and checks it for semantic consistency with the reference, weighted by the annotated solution length. PSAS-S (step level, a process evaluation): an LLM maps the model's work onto each annotated step, scores formula and value at 0.5 each, finds the first error step and classifies its error type. DeepSeek-V3 is the scorer (pp. 4-6)
human_validation: Engineering PhD candidates with physics expertise verified the translations (p. 3; App. B.1.3, p. 14). 1,000 of 8,400 model reasoning processes were manually annotated for answer correctness and first error step. Against them, PSAS reaches 98.96% (answer) and 97.23% (first error step) with Gemini-2.0-Flash and 99.35% and 98.04% with DeepSeek-V3; direct LLM evaluation reaches 87.81-93.31% and 33.18-37.54% (section 4.5 and Table 2, p. 6). The annotators were four engineering graduate students who are co-authors (App. I, p. 19).
contamination_measures: search prevention: problems whose solutions and answers a five-minute Google search finds are excluded (p. 3; App. B.1.4, p. 14); the items themselves are public exam and competition problems

engtrace_use.sentence: S-P1 (L172-177): 'While UGPhysics (Xu et al., 2025) and PhysReason (Zhang et al., 2025a) effectively test the application of reasoning to natural laws, others target advanced symbolic (...) or qualitative (...) understanding.' S-P2 (L177-180): 'Despite this progress, these benchmarks remain confined to theoretical physics, lacking the integrative context of engineering.' The section closes (S-E3, L199-201): 'Evidently, existing benchmarks remain limited to outcome matching'.
engtrace_use.explanation: S-P1 holds: PhysReason targets physics-based reasoning that requires 'physics theorems and constraints' (abstract, p. 1), and each annotated step applies a named theorem (pp. 2-4). S-P2 is loose but has some support in the paper's own limitation that it tests theorems 'under idealized conditions, rather than fully reflecting real-world physics scenarios' (p. 9). What the section leaves out matters most for EngTrace. PhysReason pairs every problem with an annotated step-by-step solution and scores model solutions step by step, including first-error-step detection, and its step scorer was validated against 1,000 manually annotated solutions (pp. 2-6). Read with S-E3, the section therefore calls a step-level benchmark outcome-only, which is the protocol's own example of misleading. The Introduction's 'no existing benchmark verifies this process' (L77-80) is scoped to engineering, so PhysReason does not contradict it; but a reviewer will treat PhysReason as the closest prior design in physics.

suggested_wording: PhysReason (Zhang et al., 2025a) evaluates the process as well as the answer: each of its 1,200 exam and olympiad physics problems carries an annotated step-by-step solution, and an LLM-based scorer grades the formula and value of each step and locates the first error. Its problems, however, are fixed, and its step scorer is an LLM checked against the authors' own annotations.
facts_to_cite: 1,200 problems: 25% knowledge-based and 75% reasoning-based, the latter in three difficulty levels; solutions average 8.1 steps, 15.6 for hard problems (p. 1)
problems are collected from college entrance exams, practice tests and international physics olympiads; those a five-minute Google search finds are excluded (p. 3)
every problem is annotated with a step-by-step solution giving the theorem, target, formula and value of each step (pp. 2-3)
PSAS-S uses an LLM to extract the model's work for each annotated step, scores formula and value equally, and locates the first error step (pp. 4-5)

on 1,000 manually annotated solutions, PSAS (DeepSeek-V3) agrees with the annotation on 99.35% of answer judgements and 98.04% of first-error-step locations; direct LLM evaluation locates the first error step correctly in 33.18-37.54% (Table 2, p. 6)
the annotators were four engineering graduate students who are co-authors (p. 19)

all 15 models score below 60% at answer level; performance falls from 75.11% on knowledge problems to 31.95% on hard problems (p. 1); step-level scores are consistently higher than answer-level scores (p. 7)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: gold step annotations with per-step values (close to EngTrace's gold traces and milestones); step-level evaluation with first-error localisation and an error taxonomy; validation of the step evaluator against human labels. Lacks: generated instances (its exam and olympiad problems are static and public, and contamination is handled only by a search filter); deterministic step checks (an LLM does both the extraction and the scoring, whereas EngTrace checks milestones and arithmetic deterministically and sends only the residue to a judge); the engineering domain (idealised physics, by its own account, p. 9); validation by independent domain experts (its annotators are four co-author graduate students, p. 19, against EngTrace's 15 own-branch experts with measured agreement). It is also multimodal (81% diagrams), which EngTrace is not.
notes: This is the physics paragraph's most important omission. PhysReason is the nearest precedent for gold step solutions combined with step-level scoring, so the revised text must say what EngTrace adds rather than claim to be first: generated instances from a private seed, deterministic milestone and digit checks, an expert-validated evaluator, and the engineering domain. 'Step Acc.' in Table 2 means accuracy in locating the first error step (caption, p. 6), not agreement on every step; do not describe it as general step-level agreement. The May reference list gets 6 of 9 first names wrong. The paper (p. 1) has Xinyu Zhang, Yuxuan Dong, Yanrui Wu, Jiaxing Huang, Chengyou Jia, Basura Fernando, Mike Zheng Shou, Lingling Zhang, Jun Liu.
